body: Public support for data centers has been rapidly waning. While data center developers initially had a free hand and many centers were approved with minimal scrutiny, this “hands off” approach is no longer the norm. In areas of the United States most impacted by the data center boom, community opposition is intense and, with growing frequency, local officials are disapproving new centers in response to grassroots pushback.

Politicians who had earlier been silent about data center impacts are now speaking up. While Democratic officeholders have been the most outspoken, Republicans too are increasingly uncomfortable with greenlighting new data centers without protections for communities. Concerns about data centers do not necessarily signify opposition to artificial intelligence (AI) technology. However, as midterm elections approach, candidates are seizing on data center concerns to stoke existing populist anger against large technology companies and the growing centrality of AI in American life.1

At the national level, the U.S. Congress is considering bipartisan legislation that would protect electricity users from bearing the costs of supplying power to data centers and connecting them to the grid.2 This legislation is a modest step in the right direction, but does not go far enough. A bolder approach, supported by some in Congress, is to impose a national moratorium on new data center development. Moratoria have been adopted by many local jurisdictions. Two states, New York and Texas, have already paused data center construction,3 and others may follow.

A nationwide moratorium would allow us to assess the full ramifications of the data center boom before we embark on a new wave of construction. Based on this assessment, Congress could enact guardrails for data center development that protect our environment and national electricity grid. Without a national framework for future data center development, we risk having a patchwork of state and local policies that could have unintended and harmful effects on our environment, economy, and power supply system as a whole.

Data centers have an outsized economic, energy, and environmental footprint.4 They consume massive amounts of electricity, and our grid is already struggling to meet the spike in demand from currently operating facilities. Without a major overhaul of the policies that govern the grid, a new surge in electricity demand from data centers threatens to overwhelm supply, causing the grid to struggle and perhaps crash during periods of peak demand, creating widespread disruption for businesses and families.

Equally troubling, increased energy demand by data centers is already resulting in a surge of new natural gas generation, and the Donald Trump Administration is promoting greater reliance on coal-fired power plants. With this resurgence of fossil fuels, emissions of dangerous pollutants and greenhouse gases will soar, degrading air quality and accelerating climate change. Data center expansion may also deplete regional water supplies because of the escalating demand for cooling water to safely operate servers and other equipment. And the massive size of many new data centers is now colliding with competing land use priorities, undermining more sustainable development strategies that protect the U.S. quality of life.

In short, the exponential increase in data center construction predicted over the next two decades is unsustainable and, if unchecked, will likely have catastrophic environmental and economic consequences.

It would be reckless to make an unconditional commitment to data center expansion on this scale without understanding these consequences and developing a national strategy to prevent them. A nationwide moratorium would give us breathing space to step back and examine where the data center boom is taking us and how to mitigate its negative impacts before they are a fait accompli.
I. Data Center Proliferation

The digital revolution has produced many breakthrough technologies, but AI is by far the most transformative and is already redefining how we work and live. There is an ongoing public debate about the pitfalls and benefits of AI. But thousands of data centers—a core part of the AI ecosystem—were built with little advance notice or public discussion. Despite the hype surrounding AI itself, few people understood that its deployment would require the rapid spread of industrial-scale facilities housing dense concentrations of servers, computer chips, integrated circuits, networking equipment, transformers, switchgear, and lithium-ion batteries.5 Now, the reality of data centers is sinking in.

Over the last 10 years, U.S. data center construction has progressed at breathtaking speed, far outpacing growth in all other countries including China, our closest competitor for AI dominance.6 According to surveys,7 there are now 4,700-5,400 U.S. data centers, vastly more than a decade ago. As of July 2026, 1,086 U.S. data centers were under construction or planned.8
It is projected that the United States will have over 6,000-7,000 data centers by 20309 ; in 2050, the number is estimated to be 15,000-20,000.10
A large portion of the new facilities will be “hyperscalers,” massive building complexes occupying several acres with extremely large computing capabilities.11 Because these
hyperscalers
are heavy electricity users, data centers in the pipeline are expected to
require four times the amount of power
as facilities operating today (255,379 megawatts (MW), compared to 61,644 MW for current data centers)
II. Rising Local Opposition

Recent polling by POLITICO found that 41% of Americans would oppose a data center being built within three miles of where they live,13 up from 28% in January 2026. The percentage supporting those projects dropped during the same period, from 37% to 24%. A March Gallup poll found that 70% of people opposed data centers in their areas, with 39% of Republicans saying they were strongly opposed.14

A recent report by the tracking service Data Center Watch determined that, in the first quarter of 2026, at least 75 projects valued at $130 billion were disrupted by local opposition.15 The report also found that, during the first six weeks of 2026, more than 300 state data center bills were filed across the United States, with proposals for statewide moratoria introduced in 14 states by legislators from both sides of the aisle. One company now bases its business model on tracking local restrictions and opposition, selling the “political risk” data it collects to data center developers.16

Two recent examples of data center rejections in Virginia’s Prince William County—part of the Northern Virginia data center hub, the largest in the nation—illustrate the influence of grassroots sentiment in blocking new projects. On July 7, 2026, county supervisors voted unanimously17 to withhold approval of Dulles South Innovation Center, a massive development on more than 1,900 acres that would turn a rural area of small farms and large-lot homes into 43 million square feet of data centers.18 Five days earlier, a lawsuit filed by local residents scuttled the Prince William Digital Gateway,19 a data center complex that would have brought as many as 37 data centers to the edge of Manassas National Battlefield Park and had been described as the largest data center development in the world.

Local leaders’ comments about the two rejected projects were telling. One county supervisor termed the size of the Dulles South project “obscene,” and explained that “I did some math. We’re dropping 15 Empire State Buildings into a rural area. Make it make sense. I can’t, I can’t.”20 The supervisor added that the project was “a pernicious health threat to everybody in this room.”21 The county’s U.S. representative said:

Our community made it clear that the energy costs and water usage for a project of this size would be a disaster . . . The fight isn’t over in our region when it comes to data center overreach, but the community has made it clear: When it comes to data centers, enough is enough.22
III. Energy Affordability

It’s not surprising that the contribution of data centers to rising electricity bills has become a flashpoint for local communities. The Consumer Price Index for electricity has surged by 6.7% year-over-year and by 41% overall since January 2020, higher than the rate of inflation over this period.23 This increase comes at a time of growing national anxiety about “affordability,” a concern that already includes energy prices along with the rising costs of other basic goods and services.24

Data centers are voracious consumers of electricity, pushing up U.S. energy demand at a regional and national level after a long period of stable and often declining energy use.25 About 4% of all U.S. electricity in 2025 was consumed by data centers,26 and multiple independent forecasts show this share rising sharply—potentially doubling or tripling over the next decade depending on AI-driven load growth. By 2026-2027, data centers are expected to consume 6-8% of all U.S. electricity, with the data center share increasing to 8-12% by 2030 and 10-18% by 2050.27 According to one projection, data centers will account for 50% of all U.S. load growth through 2030,28 meaning that half of all increases in U.S. power production will be data center-driven.

The costs of building new power plants and grid interconnections to serve data centers will be staggering, totaling hundreds of billions of dollars.29 Consumers are concerned about not only the magnitude of these costs, but whether they will be distributed equitably among ratepayers. Activist groups and local officials have repeatedly warned that utility rate-bases may subsidize grid improvements and capacity additions that serve data centers but not the public at large, giving wealthy data center developers a free ride while hard-up ratepayers pay more for electricity.30
IV. Depletion of Water Supplies

Another growing grassroots concern is the huge quantity of water required by data centers to cool servers and other equipment. According to studies, a 150-MW hyperscale data center using evaporative cooling consumes roughly 340,000 gallons per day—or about 124 million gallons per year.31

It is estimated that U.S. data centers used 17.4 billion gallons of water in 2023 and that consumption will reach 38-73 billion gallons by 2028. Indirectly, data center growth will also increase cooling water requirements at power plants as new fossil fuel generating capacity is built to power data centers.32 Technologies like closed-loop water recycling can reduce water consumption and safeguard local water resources but may require increased energy utilization, imposing higher energy costs and increasing power plant air emissions.33
By siphoning off water from public systems, data centers may add to water scarcity in regions with constrained supplies.

34 In this event, not only would water bills be higher but, in the worst case, it may be necessary to impose rationing or other curbs on water use, placing severe hardships on businesses and residents.
V. The Congressional and White House Response

The community voices raising the alarm about data centers are finding an audience in Washington, D.C. President Trump has been a vocal supporter of data centers and unfettered AI, but has tried to defuse grassroots concern about escalating energy costs through his voluntary Ratepayer Protection Pledge.35 This Pledge would commit data center developers and technology companies to cover the incremental increases in electricity costs tied to new power capacity serving data center electricity demand. Some 200 companies and nearly all Republican state governors have now signed the Pledge36; however, critics have cautioned that it is unenforceable and lacks mechanisms to track whether data center owners are meeting their commitments.37

To fill this void, both houses of Congress are now working on the Ratepayer Protection Act, bipartisan legislation requiring states to consider adopting a federal standard that would compel data centers to pay the total cost of new generation and transmission upgrades to connect them to the grid, protecting consumers from bearing these costs through their electricity bills.38 The U.S. House of Representatives Energy and Commerce Committee recently approved the bill unanimously, and it may reach the House floor later this year.39
VI. The Need to Do More

While supporting this legislation, some leading Democrats, along with advocates, community groups, and state legislators, are warning that it fails to address the full range of data center concerns and calling for more ambitious action.40 A proposal gaining traction is a nationwide moratorium on data center construction,41 similar to the one adopted by New York Gov. Kathy Hochul42 and now by Texas Gov. Greg Abbott.43 Rep. Frank Pallone (D-N.J.), the influential ranking minority member of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, recently backed this concept. Warning that “We’re seeing electricity prices sky rocketing, the grid is strained, and there is also a lot of concern about clean air and water pollution, and most states don’t have anything on the books,” Pallone said “there needs to be guardrails” to address these concerns but, “if we can’t achieve that, then the possibility of a moratorium out there is certainly real.”44

A pause in data center construction is anathema to those who, like the president, believe the United States is in an existential race with China for global AI hegemony and will lose that race if we pull back from rapid buildout of data centers.45 But even without a moratorium, we can’t assume the path ahead for new data centers will be smooth and seamless.

VII. Crashing the Grid
The fears of data center opponents are not merely hypothetical concerns of hand-wringing alarmists. The threat of data centers to our electrical supply systems is real and imminent.
We know the rapid
increase in
data center
construction
projected over the next 15 years
will demand dramatic increases in energy supply.
If we can’t quickly grow that supply, electric utilities that are already struggling to manage supply-and-demand imbalances will be unable to serve their customers.
Grid
operator
s with constrained
reserve
margins will
then
be hard-pressed
to maintain system reliability,
and blackouts
, brownouts, and other disruptions in service
may be more frequent and widespread.

Even if sufficient new generation capacity is constructed and connected to the grid, the costs will be huge and, if passed on to ratepayers, will accelerate electricity price increases and raise the rate of inflation.

Convergence of these factors could precipitate a national energy crisis similar to the oil shocks of the 1970s. Because of political gridlock and long-standing structural flaws in our energy supply system, the United States is grossly unprepared to meet a new surge in electricity demand. In several regions, our electricity grid is now barely meeting rising power needs during periods of peak demand. The PJM interconnection,46 the grid operator for the heavily populated Mid-Atlantic region and parts of the Midwest, is home to more data centers than any other region.47 But PJM’s power reserves are already too small to meet reliability requirements,48 and during a recent summer heat wave, power demand reached 163 gigawatts (GW),49 the secondhighest level on record, and would have been higher if PJM had not ordered curtailments of energy use.

PJM has acknowledged that significant new capacity is needed just to meet the energy needs of data centers now operating,50 and it projects that data centers alone will add over 30 GW of additional peak electricity demand by 2030.51 In Virginia, the national epicenter of data center construction and part of PJM, Dominion Energy, the dominant utility, has estimated that new data centers in the pipeline will need 70,000 MW of power if they come online.52

Worried power suppliers and federal and state energy regulators are well aware of PJM’s vulnerabilities and working overtime to remedy them.53 But the challenges are immense and there are few fixes that are readily implementable.

PJM’s woes are not unique. The Electric Reliability Council of Texas, another hotbed of data center development, just announced that demand on the state’s main power grid could nearly double in the next five to six years, almost entirely due to new data centers, and that only a fraction of that demand could be met using available or projected power generation.55 In response, Republican Governor Abbott halted new applications to connect data centers to the grid.56

At the national level, policymakers understand that growth in electricity demand cannot be met unless we reform our energy supply system to address its deeply rooted shortcomings.57 These include lack of incentives and drivers for building new transmission lines across state lines; delays in building interconnections that give new load centers access to the grid; logjams in permitting and environmental approvals; and inadequate federal and state funding for investments in grid modernization. These issues are unresolved not because Congress isn’t trying, but because they are complex and politically divisive and longterm solutions are difficult to design and implement.
VIII. Meeting the Environmental Challenges

Even if the obstacles to growing our energy supply could be addressed and energy cost increases held in check, the data center boom would present another challenge: how do we manage the environmental impacts of building hundreds of new sources of electricity?

The consequences of large-scale water consumption are potentially far-reaching, yet we lack a body of data on current rates of water use by data centers, what conservation measures are in use, how water supplies might be affected in areas with high concentrations of data centers, and the pros and cons of different water-cooling technologies. Nor do we have reliable estimates of the anticipated increases in water consumption from a large expansion of the data center universe. Although we could be on the cusp of a dramatic rise in water utilization by data centers,
we have no national guidelines and best practices for sustainable water use by data center operators.
We are similarly lacking in understanding of how the data center boom will affect air quality.

Numerous new natural gas plants have been announced to serve data centers,58 and the Trump Administration is calling for extending the service lines of existing coal plants and building new coal-fired generation.59 Heavy reliance on these fossil fuels to provide power to data centers is projected to cause a dramatic spike in emissions of pollutants that cause lung disease and other adverse health effects.60 It will also raise U.S. emissions of greenhouse gases that contribute to climate change.

New “behind the grid” fossil-fueled generating units built and operated on the same sites as data centers (an approach that President Trump has encouraged in lieu of connecting to the grid61) could bring pollution into local communities, often without in-depth assessments of its consequences for air quality.
Indeed, large on-site concentrations of diesel and natural gas turbines are already spurring pollution concerns in communities downwind of data centers.62

The least-polluting options for new generation to power data centers are wind, solar, and maybe nuclear, supported by new transmission systems and more reliance on advanced energy storage technologies.

But the president and his subordinates appear fixated on promoting more coal and natural gas, and are implacably opposed to expanding renewable power.63 As a result, numerous new wind and solar projects have been blocked.64

In this environment, utilities and developers choosing power sources for new data centers appear to be shunning renewables in favor of fossil fuels, locking in long-term dependence on these energy sources and the accompanying degradation of air quality, harm to public health, and climate change.
Here too, decisions made today without studies of long-term air emission impacts and policies encouraging clean power alternatives will have irreversible consequences that later cannot be undone.
IX. Can We Afford to Slow Down AI?

Driving the data center boom is the technology industry’s investment of mind-boggling sums (ultimately estimated to exceed three trillion dollars65) to create the computing capacity needed to infuse AI into all spheres of the economy and American life.66 Investments on this massive scale are unprecedented in U.S. economic history. AI supporters argue that, like previous breakthrough technologies, these massive investments will not only enrich investors but boost our standard of living and spread new wealth throughout our society.

However, AI proponents have not made an effective case for its broad-based benefits. Because of the industry’s penchant for secrecy, communities have been in the dark about how proposed data centers will be used and even who will operate them or purchase their services. This information vacuum is preventing us from making informed judgments on whether AI’s potential economic and societal benefits justify the adverse impacts of data centers. Without carefully weighing these cost-benefit trade offs, it would be a mistake to assume that slowing down data center development will necessarily harm our economic future. Since the benefits of AI and their timing are poorly understood, we should not take them on faith.

Indeed, Silicon Valley leaders are themselves deeply ambivalent about AI’s explosive growth, and many are calling for it to be slowed down. A recent petition from over 1,000 AI engineers and executives warned that AI capabilities are rapidly accelerating “beyond our ability to understand or control the resulting systems,” and that the U.S. government should lead “an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development.”67 While these concerns relate to the pitfalls of AI itself, they apply equally to the dangers of unrestricted buildout of data centers without understanding and addressing their energy and environmental impacts.
X. Avoiding a Patchwork of State and Local Approaches

Some are concerned that a national data center moratorium would curtail the autonomy of state and local governments and impose a federal solution on elected officials who want to choose their own paths for balancing community concerns with development pressures.68

But as more and more data centers are put on hold due to local opposition, environmental concerns, and electricity and water supply constraints, the consequences are being felt across the United States and inaction by the federal government is becoming increasingly untenable.
The current decentralized system, with its patchwork of approaches and requirements, lacks consistency and may have unintended and harmful consequences at the national level.
For example,

if some states freeze data center construction, developers will turn to other states that are willing to cut deals with technology companies at the expense of communities and the environment in order to attract economic development and tax revenue. Indeed, such a “race to the bottom” is already occurring in Louisiana and other states where huge projects are moving forward in secrecy and without safeguards for communities.69

Equally important, our electricity grid is managed at a regional and national scale, and locally driven energy supply choices may wreak havoc on the availability of power and cost of electricity in other states and regions.

The same is true for our environment; emissions of traditional pollutants and greenhouse gases have public health consequences across state boundaries. This is why our environmental laws are nationwide in application and impose baseline protections of air and water quality throughout the country.

To allow energy and environmental policy choices that have national implications to devolve to state and local governments would undermine the level playing field that has traditionally created a foundation for U.S. economic growth.
A nationwide moratorium would provide
breathing

and managing data center

This would be a daunting challenge for our leaders in Congress and the executive branch, but the current situation is unsustainable and the policy vacuum must be filled.
XI. Conclusion
Unless the public has confidence that government is responsibly managing data center expansion and it will provide net benefits to society,
communities and local governments will continue to take matters into their own hands, slowing and even halting data center development even without a formal moratorium.

A crash effort to build new data centers without a credible plan for meeting their voracious demand for energy will risk the collapse of the grid and create more angry confrontations between communities and developers. Many planned data centers will either not be built or fail to operate.

A timeout on data center construction will provide the space to determine how many new data centers are needed for a sustainable AI future and how we can pace their development to align with our long-term energy and environmental goals.
